cells.tense: The reading stays steady and it keeps getting sharper the longer you sit with it.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you notice about a situation you're in, and let it stand without a verdict for a week. Try it even while the picture stays open.
cells.core:
You can be inside a situation and still see it whole. That double view — in the room and above it — is yours, and it holds. You pick up what's actually going on before anyone names it, and it doesn't cost you your place in the group.
What keeps it clean is that the read stays open. You see far enough to move, and you don't slam the case shut. You let the next step arrive on its own and then take it. Someone else in your spot would call it done by now, or keep second-guessing past the point of usefulness. You do neither. That's the balance — a clear read that keeps getting clearer without hardening into a final word.
cells.sheetLine: You see the whole pattern and leave room for it to grow.
cells.verb: seeing the whole pattern — what's true across every layer
cells.place: in the middle of not knowing, walking by the next patch of light

cells.tense: You are already living in a verdict the situation hasn't finished writing yet.
cells.ask: Pick one situation you've already decided. Say out loud that you could be wrong, then do one thing only a right read would justify.
cells.core:
You can see a pattern forming before anyone else in the room can. That's the read working. When it's clean you hold it and stay curious; the picture keeps sharpening in your hands and you let it.
Where you've gone instead is ahead of it. The read hardens into a verdict, and the verdict has to be defended, so you push it on people who haven't caught up. It stops being a read and becomes a stance. The certainty feels like clarity from the inside. From where others stand, it's a door closing. Your read may well be right. The timing is the part out of step.

cells.tense: You stand in the room where a read could land, and you keep the ground open.
cells.ask: Name one thing you see clearly to one person, out loud, and let their response stand without arguing it either way.
cells.core:
You can hold a pattern in view long enough to say something true about it. That's what's here, and it's present. When it's working it looks like a plain sentence offered once and let land — said, then left open to whatever comes back.
Where you are now, the options keep turning over and none of them settles. Each new angle gets examined before the last one has been tried. Part of you may be waiting for the picture to close on its own; part of you may be guarding something you'd rather not test. Either way the pattern stays legible and unspoken, and the searching has become the place you live.

cells.tense: You are reading the pattern right now and talking about it as something that simply happened.
cells.ask: Name one read you've been making lately, say out loud that you're the one making it, and check it with someone before you act on it.
cells.core:
You're reading what's going on around you all day long. It shows in what you say and what you leave out, in small calls you make without counting them as calls. The read is working. What isn't happening is you standing behind it.
That's the catch. A read that doesn't feel like yours can't be tested, because who would test the facts? So it runs uncorrected — mostly right, occasionally off, and you're the last to hear when it's off. When this is clean, it looks like a plain claim on your own read, offered once and put where someone can check it. Start there. One read, named as yours, before you build anything on it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already reading the room. You just haven't claimed it.

attempts.check: The record supports Recognition seated in Imagination, but for Too Little I invented that the last time saying it out loud went badly — the record only locates someone still standing at a door already behind them, and says nothing about what happened there or who was in the room. A reader could reasonably say they have simply never felt the call yet. The ask survives a wrong read either way: naming out loud the truth already seen, and testing it, teaches something whether the hesitation is one bad experience or no felt call at all. The line that would serve the writer more than them is any sentence that tells them what happened when they last tried.
